_meta.purpose: Plants we might bring back to Fernwood. Distinct from plants.json — that file tracks what is on the property; this file tracks what could be. Per the depth filter, every candidate has to fit Fernwood's actual reality: 2,959 ft Blue Ridge, zone 6b, Cove Forest + Low-to-Mid Elevation Oak Forest mosaic with potential Seepage Wetlands in the spring drainage.
_meta.communityReference: Natural Communities of Blue Ridge Ecoregion (GNPS, adapted from Edwards, Ambrose, Kirkman 2013 UGA Press)

categories.restoration: Multi-decade canopy / regional restoration species. Slow, relational (TACF, HRI). Most ecologically meaningful.
categories.keystone: Tallamy-defined keystone genera for Blue Ridge ecoregion — species that support disproportionate caterpillar / Lepidoptera diversity (oaks 400+, cherries 450+, willows 380+).
categories.rich-cove: Special-concern flora of the rich cove community. Look-don't-pick if found on the property; if planting, only ethical-propagation sources.
categories.cultivar-trial: Native genus with a published Mt. Cuba Center trial; the trial winner is the defensible cultivar pick.
categories.bird-pollinator: Strong wildlife value — Audubon Plants for Birds + Xerces Southeast pollinator list + NWF Native Plant Finder zip 30143.
categories.native-grass: Native bunchgrasses and graminoids for understory, forest edge, or seepage zones.

candidates.name: Autumn bentgrass
candidates.rationale: Native perennial bunchgrass, partial shade, mesic to wet soils. Fits the spring drainage seepage zone and forest-edge mesic spots. Soft fine-textured groundcover with late-season inflorescences. Flagged for inclusion by Mom.
candidates.notes: Not in the GNPS Blue Ridge landscaping matrix, but iNaturalist + Native Plant Trust + Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center all confirm the species' habitat (mesic to dry forests, seepage swamps, depressions) matches the property. Bunchgrass habit, no rhizomes or stolons — gentle in a planted setting. 8-31 inches tall.

candidates.name: American chestnut
candidates.rationale: Once a dominant canopy species at this elevation in the southern Appalachians. The blight (introduced 1904) killed virtually all mature trees from Maine to Georgia by 1950. One of the two big landowner-participation restoration species. This slope was once chestnut canopy.
candidates.notes: This is a multi-year commitment, not a sale-stand purchase. TACF GA's own framing: "Many trees today may not carry sufficient disease resistance, so most likely will not live to become the 'mighty giants' we all hope and dream about." Path is national membership → Potential Orchard Steward form → stewardship plan with GA Science Coordinator → germplasm agreement. They recommend a few years of membership + volunteering before planting. Smaller path: pure American chestnut seedlings at the annual spring sale. Most ecologically meaningful candidate on this list; also the slowest and least guaranteed.

attribution.author: The original uploader was Peatcher at German Wikipedia.

candidates.name: Eastern hemlock
candidates.rationale: Cool-drainage native, occurs in acidic Cove Forest sites. Likely already present on the property in the spring drainage. Threatened by Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (HWA) since 2003 in Georgia; statewide by 2012. No other native conifer fills hemlock's ecological role.
candidates.notes: ACTIONABLE NOW: check existing hemlocks on the property for HWA and treat (imidacloprid + dinotefuran soil drench at root flare). HRI has DIY landowner instructions. FUTURE / NOT YET AVAILABLE: resistant-stock plantings for forest restoration — HRI's genetic-resistance work is still early-stage and there is no current sourcing pathway for landowners. Two ornamental landscape cultivars ('Traveler', 'Crossroads') are expected to be released for purchase "in the near future" but are explicitly landscape-only, not forest restoration stock. Step 1 is the only step worth taking this year.

candidates.name: Flame azalea
candidates.rationale: Signature North Georgia mountain native — the Cohutta and Smokies range is centered on this species. Brilliant May-June bloom. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge landscaping list for both Montane Oak and Cove Forest understory.
candidates.notes: If sourcing from Gardens of the Blue Ridge: they specialize in native azaleas including hard-to-find color forms. Drainage matters — happiest on sloped, well-drained, acidic soil.

candidates.name: White oak
candidates.rationale: The keystone genus per Tallamy. Each oak supports 400+ Lepidoptera species — the foundation for nearly every songbird's nesting season. Confirmed in Low-to-Mid Elevation Oak Forest community at this elevation.
candidates.notes: GFC seedling sale typically offers multiple oak species at landowner-scale quantities and prices. December-March planting. If choosing one keystone tree to plant first, this is the answer.

candidates.name: Smooth (wild) hydrangea
candidates.rationale: Native to Georgia coves, including this elevation. Mt. Cuba Center's wild hydrangea trial (2022) found 'Haas' Halo' the top performer in the Mid-Atlantic — directly applicable to the property. Sits cleanly alongside the existing hydrangea entries on plants.json.
candidates.notes: The existing plants.json hydrangea entries are mixed natives + Hydrangea macrophylla (non-native). Adding 'Haas' Halo' is a clean way to deepen the native component without removing what's planted. Mt. Cuba's full trial report: mtcubacenter.org/trials/hydrangea/

candidates.name: 'Claire Grace' wild bergamot
candidates.rationale: M. fistulosa is widely native including the north Georgia mountains. Mt. Cuba Center's monarda trial (40 selections, 3 years) named 'Claire Grace' the clear winner — 3-week floral display, 130+ butterfly and moth visits over the trial, strong powdery-mildew resistance. The defensible monarda pick.
candidates.notes: Pollinator workhorse for a sunny-to-part-shade bed. Pairs naturally with cardinal flower for a hummingbird + butterfly combination. Mt. Cuba report: mtcubacenter.org/trials/monarda/

candidates.name: 'Screamin' Yellow' yellow wild indigo
candidates.rationale: Top performer in Mt. Cuba Center's baptisia trial (46 selections, 2012-2015). Long-lived perennial with a deep taproot, drought-tolerant once established. Bright yellow spring spikes.
candidates.notes: Range honesty: B. sphaerocarpa is south-central US native, not strictly a Blue Ridge mountain species. If a regional-native is preferred over the trial winner, the same Mt. Cuba trial's 'Purple Smoke' (a hybrid of B. australis × B. alba) hits the same garden function and B. australis IS native to the southern Appalachians. Either way: full sun, well-drained — not for the forest interior.

candidates.name: 'Pica Bella' purple coneflower
candidates.rationale: E. purpurea is native to the eastern US including north Georgia woodland edges and open glades. Mt. Cuba Center's coneflower trial (75 selections, 2018-2020) named 'Pica Bella' the top performer; 'Fragrant Angel' averaged the most butterfly visits.
candidates.notes: 12 cultivars rated outstanding (4.3+/5) — defensible alternatives if 'Pica Bella' isn't available. Avoid the heavily-bred doubles and orange/yellow color novelties; Mt. Cuba's trial showed they underperform on both vigor and pollinator visits. Mt. Cuba report: mtcubacenter.org/trials/echinacea-mid-atlantic-region/

candidates.name: 'Summer Sunshine' swamp coreopsis
candidates.rationale: Top performer in Mt. Cuba Center's coreopsis trial (94 selections) — disease-resistant foliage, late-season floral display. The defensible coreopsis pick from the published trial.
candidates.notes: Range honesty: C. palustris is a coastal-plain wetland species, not native to the Blue Ridge mountains. The pond and spring drainage could host it if the trial winner is preferred. For a Fernwood-region-native alternative, C. verticillata 'Zagreb' (threadleaf coreopsis) IS Blue Ridge native and was also a Mt. Cuba top performer — better fit for dry sunny spots.

candidates.name: Pink lady's slipper
candidates.rationale: Native orchid; rich-cove special-concern species. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge Cove Forest list. If found on the property, leave alone and support — do not transplant. If planting, only from ethical-propagation sources (never wild-collected).
candidates.notes: Mycorrhizal-dependent — moves poorly. ABG Safeguarding Nursery is the propagation partner for any rare-species restoration thread. Worth walking the north-facing slopes in May to look for the existing colony before considering sourcing.

candidates.name: Cardinal flower
candidates.rationale: Pond-edge and seepage native; the strongest hummingbird-attractor in eastern North America. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge Seepage Wetland list. Direct fit for the pond area and the spring drainage.
candidates.notes: Short-lived perennial but self-sows freely in suitable conditions. Pair with great blue lobelia (Lobelia siphilitica) for blue + red pollinator bed.

candidates.name: Christmas fern
candidates.rationale: Year-round evergreen native fern — confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge Low-to-Mid Oak Forest list. Excellent winter texture in the woodland understory; hosts insects that overwinter and feed early-spring birds.
candidates.notes: One of the easiest natives to establish under existing tree canopy. UGA Extension B 987-2 (Ferns) is the deep reference.

candidates.name: Common witchhazel
candidates.rationale: Native understory shrub / small tree. Yellow-strap-petaled flowers in October-November when virtually nothing else is blooming — important late-season pollinator resource. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge list across Cove, Low-Mid Oak, and Seepage communities.
candidates.notes: Distinct from the spring-blooming Asian witch hazels common in nursery trade. The late-season bloom is the diagnostic feature. Slow to establish but very long-lived.
